clue.text: Vaulting judge controlling contest in heartless fashion

indicators.note: something heartless has lost its centre, so the middle letters of the phrase before it are cut out

parts.note: J is the standard abbreviation for judge
an umpire controls a match or contest

explanation.surface: A judge oversees a pole-vault event without any warmth or enthusiasm.
explanation.walkthrough: UMPIRING has eight letters, so its heart is the middle pair IR; dropping them leaves UMPING.
explanation.definitionFit: Vaulting is leaping over something, so the two participles are synonyms.

clue.text: Biased article appearing in Paris Match

parts.note: un is the French indefinite article, the one a Parisian uses
to match something is to equal it; an equal is also a match

explanation.surface: A slanted piece runs in the French magazine Paris Match.
explanation.walkthrough: Paris Match is a real French weekly; here 'Paris' only tells you the article is French.
explanation.definitionFit: An unequal contest or treatment is one-sided, which is what a biased one is.

clue.text: One's attached to horse

definitions.meaning: first meaning, read as two words: something you ... is what a thing is attached to
second meaning: a piebald or spotted horse

explanation.surface: Someone has grown fond of a horse.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as PIN TO: a pinned item is attached to something.
explanation.definitionFit: A pinto is a horse with patchy markings, popular in the American West.

clue.text: Lexicon or dictionary? It's more than enough for Scandinavian

indicators.note: the phrase holds more letters than needed, so the answer sits inside it with spare letters on either side

parts.note: running across the end of the first word, the whole second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Someone asks which reference book suits a Scandinavian reader and is told either would be plenty.
explanation.definitionFit: Nordic describes the peoples and countries of northern Europe, a near synonym of Scandinavian.

clue.text: Spreads offered by boring building society, say

indicators.note: a word boring through another drills into its middle, so it sits inside

parts.note: BS is the abbreviation for building society
to say something is to utter it

explanation.surface: A dull building society hands out spreads, perhaps sandwich fillings.
explanation.walkthrough: A building society is a British savings-and-mortgage lender; 'boring' looks like dull but means drilling in.
explanation.definitionFit: Butter is a spread, and as a verb 'butters' also means spreads, as on toast.

clue.text: Museum moving diamonds, admitting number yet to be counted

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so the next piece goes inside
things that are moving are being shifted around, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
D is the card-suit abbreviation for diamonds
N is the abbreviation for number

explanation.surface: A museum relocating its diamonds takes in a number of pieces nobody has yet tallied.
explanation.walkthrough: The shuffled letters form USUMMED, and N goes in after the first U.
explanation.definitionFit: To sum is to add up, so something unsummed has not yet been totalled.

clue.text: Increasingly dry river being crossed by this stage

indicators.note: something crossed by another has it running through, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for river
a tier is a level or stage

explanation.surface: At this point the river is crossed, and the landscape is getting more parched.
explanation.definitionFit: Thirstier is the comparative of thirsty, meaning more in need of drink, so increasingly dry.

clue.text: Surgeon in Guard regularly fixed up messengers

indicators.note: in a down clue, putting letters up means writing them bottom to top
regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: first, third, fifth letters and so on

explanation.surface: A surgeon serving in the Guards patched up the dispatch riders.
explanation.walkthrough: Guard is a regiment, but here it is only a source of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Runners were people sent on foot to carry messages, hence messengers.

clue.text: It could bePenn and Teller's cut short?

indicators.note: a teller is someone who tells, speaking out loud, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: shorn means cut, as hair is cut short

explanation.surface: Penn and Teller, the American magic double act, might have their hair trimmed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penn and Teller' reads as the magicians, but Penn is the actor Sean Penn and the teller is a speaker. In a non-rhotic British accent, shorn and Sean sound alike. The source prints 'bePenn' without a space.
explanation.definitionFit: Sean is a first name, and the actor Sean Penn is its best-known bearer, so Penn is an example.

clue.text: Fish with reason to change, changes

indicators.note: the letters are told to change, so they are reordered

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone fishes for a reason to change and makes changes.
explanation.definitionFit: To refashion something is to remake it in a new form, so the verb means alters.

clue.text: Lively around mid-May, like the Highlands?

indicators.note: one piece goes around the other, enclosing it

parts.note: Scottish mountains are bens, and the Highlands are packed with them

indicators.note: mid- points to the centre letter of the word it is attached to

parts.note: the centre of a three-letter word

explanation.surface: Someone feels lively around the middle of May, as the Highlands do in spring.
explanation.walkthrough: Ben is the Scottish word for a mountain, as in Ben Nevis.
explanation.definitionFit: Full of beans is an idiom for energetic and high-spirited.

clue.text: One cutting Ancient Egyptian exam class

parts.note: Tutankhamun, the boy pharaoh, often called King Tut

indicators.note: a piece cutting into another slices into its middle, so sits inside

parts.note: an oral is a spoken examination
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: An ancient Egyptian carver sits an exam class.
explanation.definitionFit: A tutorial is a small teaching session, a kind of class.

clue.text: Man is entering name back to front

indicators.note: a piece entering another goes inside it
the back letter is moved to the front, shifting the word round by one

parts.note: a term is a name for something
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man fills in a form with his name written backwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back to front' suggests reversing TERM, but only its last letter moves to the front, giving MTER.
explanation.definitionFit: Mister is the title given to a man, and is used informally to address one.

clue.text: Player in game, fly-half possibly, crossing line

indicators.note: a piece crossing another straddles it, so the other sits within

parts.note: in rugby the fly-half is one of the backs
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A rugby fly-half crosses the try line during a game.
explanation.walkthrough: The rugby setting makes 'player' look like a team member; it is a side in chess or draughts.
explanation.definitionFit: In chess and draughts one side is Black, and it is the second player to move.

clue.text: Student constrained by awful English record

indicators.note: something constrained is hemmed in, so it sits inside the other pieces

parts.note: in British slang chronic means very bad
L for learner, as on British learner-driver plates
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A student stuck with a dreadful English report.
explanation.definitionFit: A chronicle is a historical account of events in order, so a record.

clue.text: Very becoming knight, most attractive — or least popular?

indicators.note: one thing becoming another turns into it, so one letter is swapped for another

parts.note: the superlative of lovely
V is the abbreviation for very
N is knight in chess notation

explanation.surface: A very becoming knight might be the most attractive, or the least popular.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very becoming' reads as very flattering, but the words split: V becomes N in the most attractive word.
explanation.definitionFit: Lonely people have few companions, so the loneliest is the one with the fewest friends.

clue.text: Experts maybe freezing bananas if Celsius drops

indicators.note: a letter that drops falls out of the word

parts.note: freezing means very cold
a bunch of bananas is called a hand
C is the abbreviation for Celsius

explanation.surface: Experts might be freezing bananas if the temperature drops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bananas' looks like 'mad', but a cluster of bananas on the stem is a hand.
explanation.definitionFit: An old hand is an idiom for a veteran with long experience.

clue.text: Byzantine atlas bore model of the heavens

indicators.note: byzantine means intricately tangled, so the letters are knotted into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An old Byzantine atlas carried a map of the sky.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests Atlas holding up the heavens.
explanation.definitionFit: An astrolabe is an old instrument representing the sky, used to find star positions.

clue.text: Proust's works: a Christmas tradition?

indicators.note: works suggests something worked over or processed, so the letters are reshaped

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Reading Proust's novels at Christmas as a family custom.
explanation.walkthrough: Brussels sprouts are a fixture of the British Christmas dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: Brussels sprouts are served on Christmas Day by custom, hence a Christmas tradition.

clue.text: General offensive undone by men retreating

indicators.note: something undone is opened up, and the other piece goes into the gap

parts.note: bad language is offensive

indicators.note: troops retreating go back the way they came, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: other ranks, ordinary soldiers as against officers

explanation.surface: A general's attack is wrecked as his soldiers fall back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'General' and 'offensive' read as a military campaign; General is an adjective here.
explanation.definitionFit: Broad and general both describe something wide-ranging rather than detailed.

clue.text: Somewhere in Liverpool area, where branch might be located

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for area
a branch is found in a tree

explanation.surface: A spot in Liverpool where a bank branch might be found.
explanation.walkthrough: Aintree is the Liverpool suburb whose racecourse hosts the Grand National steeplechase.
explanation.definitionFit: Aintree lies in the Liverpool area of Merseyside, so it is a place there.

clue.text: Poet's daughters penning lines with nurse

indicators.note: to pen is to enclose, as livestock in a pen

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for daughter, doubled for the plural
RY is railway, and railway lines
an Enrolled Nurse, a former British grade

explanation.surface: A poet's daughters write verse with the help of a nurse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penning lines' reads as writing poetry, which fits the poet; it is enclosure here.
explanation.definitionFit: John Dryden was the seventeenth-century English poet laureate.

clue.text: Force Yank to censor wife's language

parts.note: F is the physics symbol for force

indicators.note: a censor strikes out material, so a letter is removed

parts.note: to yank is to wrench, pull sharply
W is the abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: An American forces himself to bowdlerise his wife's swearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yank' looks like an American; it is the verb for pulling hard.
explanation.definitionFit: French is the language of France and of many other countries.

clue.text: Car fans excitedly describing current Continentals?

indicators.note: to describe a shape is to draw around it, so these letters go around the next piece
excited things jump about, so the letters are mixed

parts.note: taken as written
I is the physics symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: Motoring enthusiasts gush about the latest European models.
explanation.walkthrough: Continentals usually means mainland Europeans; the question mark flags that Africa is a continent too.
explanation.definitionFit: Africans are people of the continent of Africa, so continentals in a playful sense.

clue.text: Given a clown as bedtime comforter?

parts.note: Coco the Clown was a famous British circus clown
taken as written

explanation.surface: A child is handed a toy clown to cuddle at bedtime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bedtime comforter' suggests a teddy or blanket; it is a hot drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Cocoa is a hot chocolate drink traditionally taken before sleep to settle down.

clue.text: Treated with sulphur, alien dies horribly

parts.note: Vulcans are the alien race of Mr Spock in Star Trek

indicators.note: something done horribly is mangled, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An alien is treated with sulphur and dies a horrible death.
explanation.definitionFit: Vulcanising rubber means heating it with sulphur to harden it, as in tyre making.

clue.text: Cheesemaker using rennet, delivering primarily this

definitions.text: Cheesemaker using rennet, delivering primarily this

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so the opening letter of each word is taken

parts.note: the opening letters of four words

explanation.surface: A cheesemaker adds rennet and mainly produces this.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the definition and the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Rennet makes milk coagulate into curd, the solid that becomes cheese.

clue.text: Disparage Anglo-Saxon prize when it's announced

parts.note: AS is the abbreviation for Anglo-Saxon

indicators.note: something announced is spoken out, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: a purse is prize money, as in boxing

explanation.surface: Belittling an Anglo-Saxon award at its announcement.
explanation.definitionFit: To asperse is to cast slurs on someone, a literary synonym of disparage.

clue.text: Lacking sponsorship, Charlie's dropped not fired

indicators.note: a letter that is dropped is left out

parts.note: without a backer
Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A man called Charlie lost his backers and was dropped, though not sacked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fired' looks like sacked; it is the potter's or baker's sense of heated in a kiln or oven.
explanation.definitionFit: Pottery is fired in a kiln, so unbaked clay has not been fired.
